archetype.name: Better Than Its Record (process-first)
archetype.definition: Utah controls five-on-five play like a top team and runs one of the league's best power plays, but bottom-tier goaltending and a leaky penalty kill have dragged its record to the middle of the Central.

report.headline: Elite five-on-five team leaking goals through its crease and penalty kill
report.take:
On the underlying numbers, Utah is one of the best teams in the league. Its 56.8% xGF % ranks 2nd and its 53% CF % ranks 5th, so the Mammoth have the puck and win the chance battle most nights. They also allow only 25.2 shots against a game, 7th fewest. The roster grades back that up: an A- blueline and a B forward group. The power play converts 32.5%, 3rd in the league and ten points above the league average. That profile should belong to a team near the top of the Central. Instead Utah sits sixth at 12-9-3, with a goal differential of -1.

The gap comes down to two units. The goalies rank 30th at -10.3 GSAx, and the team's all-situations save % of .878 ranks 29th. Karel Vejmelka has been the main problem at .872 and -7 GSAx over 15 starts. Sebastian Cossa has been better at .886 but is still well below average. The penalty kill sits at 71.3%, 27th, which is the same story seen through special teams: few shots allowed, but the ones that get through go in. Shooting is not the issue. At 9.7% the skaters finish almost exactly at the league average, so the low PDO (98.3 at five-on-five) comes almost entirely from the save side.

The record itself reflects this. Utah went 9-5 in October, then lost six straight in November, including three overtime losses inside a 3-4-3 ten-game stretch. That is not a team being outplayed. It is a team losing one-goal games because its goalies are not making the saves an average goalie would. Pts vs Goal Diff is close to neutral at +0.6, so luck in close games is not hiding anything. The goal differential is simply worse than the process.

History points toward a recovery. Last season this same team posted a 52.4% xGF %, weaker than this year's, but got +14.1 GSAx from its goalies and still finished with 92 points. This year's five-on-five game is better and the goaltending far worse. Goaltending that poor rarely stays at the bottom of the league over a full season. Utah is on pace for 92 points again, and the rate stats suggest the upside from here is greater than the downside.

strengths.title: Top-tier five-on-five control
strengths.body: Utah ranks 2nd in xGF % and 5th in CF %, and it keeps shots against among the lowest in the league. This is driven by structure and possession rather than shooting luck, and it improves on last year's already solid 52.4% xGF %. Shot-share edges this large are among the most stable things in hockey, so expect this to hold.

strengths.title: A power play that punishes
strengths.body: At 32.5%, Utah's power play ranks 3rd, about ten points above the league average and well up from 20% last season. Some of that conversion rate will cool, because few units hold a third of their chances over a full year. Even so, the possession base suggests it stays well above average.

strengths.title: Forwards smothered defensively
strengths.body: Opposing forwards score well under their own averages against Utah, the 2nd-best mark in the league. Centers in particular get very little. Kailer Yamamoto, with a .638 xGF % and 12 points in 15 games, shows how the top forwards are tilting the ice.

concerns.title: Goaltending is sinking the season
concerns.body: Utah's goalies are 30th in GSAx and 29th in save %, which is the main reason a team with a 2nd-ranked xGF % has a negative goal differential. Vejmelka's -7 GSAx in 15 starts is the larger share of the damage. The same team got +14.1 GSAx last season, so some correction is likely. Until it arrives, though, the strong process will not show up in the standings.

concerns.title: Penalty kill near the bottom
concerns.body: A 71.3% PK ranks 27th, nearly six points below the league average and down from 78.1% last season. Part of this is goaltending, since a .878 save % shows up hardest on the kill. Opposing defensemen are also scoring well above expectation against Utah, which fits a pattern of point shots getting through.

concerns.title: November slide lost real ground
concerns.body: A six-game losing streak turned a 9-5 October into a 3-4-3 ten-game stretch. The goal differential over those ten games was clearly negative. The losses were mostly by one goal, but the standings points are gone, and Utah now trails five Central teams.

trend.note: A strong October gave way to a six-game November skid, three of them overtime losses. Back-to-back wins over Colorado and Anaheim followed, and the last five games have been much tighter defensively, at 2.6 goals allowed a game.

weekAhead.headline: Four road division games, three against elite goaltending
weekAhead.body:
Utah opens with four straight road games inside the Central, including a Nashville-Dallas back-to-back, then comes home for Montréal. Winnipeg on Monday is the clear opportunity. The Jets allow the most shots in the league, rank 23rd in xGF % and have a 24th-ranked penalty kill that Utah's power play should exploit.

After that it gets hard. Minnesota leads the division and has the league's best GSAx. Nashville and Dallas both pair top-six goaltending with penalty kills ranked 2nd and 3rd, which neutralizes Utah's best special-teams weapon. Utah will probably out-chance most of these teams, but its goalies would have to match three of the best tandems in the league to turn that into points. Montréal at home is a fairer test. The Canadiens' power play ranks 31st, a relief for Utah's kill, and they lead the league in Pts vs Goal Diff, a sign their record is running ahead of their play.

keyMatchups.title: Power play against Winnipeg's kill
keyMatchups.body: Winnipeg kills just 72.5% of penalties and gives up 31.6 shots a game, the most in the league. Utah's 3rd-ranked power play should feed on that. It is the best chance on the trip to bank two points before facing the division's top teams.

keyMatchups.title: Utah's crease against elite goalies
keyMatchups.body: Minnesota (+16.2), Dallas (+12.7) and Nashville (+8.4) all rank in the top six in GSAx, while Utah sits 30th. In tight Central games that difference decides results. Utah's possession edge has to produce enough extra chances to cover it.

keyMatchups.title: Nashville and Dallas kill penalties
keyMatchups.body: The back-to-back faces the 2nd- and 3rd-best penalty kills, at 89.1% and 88.8%. Utah's power-play edge mostly disappears in those games, so they will be decided at five-on-five, where Utah has the stronger numbers.

weekAhead.watch: Who starts in goal on the Nashville-Dallas back-to-back. If Cossa's .886 starts taking over Vejmelka's workload, that is the first sign Utah's goaltending is turning.

restOfSeason.body:
The stable parts of Utah's game are the possession and chance numbers, and they belong to a team well above .500. The unstable part is a team save % near the bottom of the league from a tandem whose team posted strong GSAx a year ago. Even partial recovery in net, toward league average, turns many of these one-goal losses into points and should lift the penalty kill along with it. The power play will likely drift down from 32.5%, but not enough to offset that.

The current pace of 92 points looks like the floor of a realistic range rather than the ceiling. I project roughly 88 to 98 points, which puts Utah in the playoff mix in a crowded Central. The downside case is that the goaltending simply stays this bad, in which case the five-on-five dominance keeps producing a .500-ish team.
swingFactors: Whether Vejmelka or Cossa climbs toward league-average save %
Penalty-kill recovery as the goaltending steadies
How much the power play cools from 32.5%

confidence.note: 24 games; process stats are reliable, but goaltending samples are noisy.
